title: Solving Zero-Sum Games with Fewer Matrix-Vector Products
authors: Ishani  Karmarkar (Stanford University, United States), Liam O'Carroll (Stanford University, United States), Aaron  Sidford (Stanford University, United States)
abstract: In this paper we consider the problem of computing an e-approximate Nash equilibrium of a zero-sum game in a payoff matrix A ∊ R^{m×n} with O(1)-bounded entries, given access to a matrix-vector product oracle for A and its transpose. We provide a deterministic algorithm that solves the problem using Õ(e^{-8/9})-oracle queries, where Õ(·) hides factors polylogarithmic in m, n, and e^{-1}. Our result improves upon the state-of-the-art query complexity of Õ(e^{-1}) established by Nemirovski (2004) and Nesterov (2005). We obtain this result through a general framework that yields improved deterministic query complexities for solving a broader class of minimax optimization problems, which includes computing a linear classifier (hard-margin support vector machine) as well as linear regression.

Abstract—In this paper we consider the problem of
computing an ϵ-approximate Nash Equilibrium of a zerosum game in a payoff matrix A ∈ Rm×n with O(1)-bounded
entries given access to a matrix-vector product oracle
for A and its transpose A⊤ . We provide a deterministic
algorithm that solves the problem using Õ(ϵ−8/9 )-oracle
queries, where Õ(·) hides factors polylogarithmic in m,
n, and ϵ−1 . Our result improves upon the state-of-the-art
query complexity of Õ(ϵ−1 ) established by [Nemirovski,
2004] and [Nesterov, 2005]. We obtain this result through
a general framework that yields improved deterministic
query complexities for solving a broader class of minimax
optimization problems which includes computing a linear
classifier (hard-margin support vector machine) as well as
linear regression.1
Index Terms—zero-sum games, matrix-vector games,
support vector machines, regression, query complexity

to maximize the expected payoff.
A common approximate solution concept for zero-sum
games is that of an ϵ-Nash equilibrium. Intuitively, at an
ϵ-Nash equilibrium, the minimization and maximization
players pick strategies x ∈ ∆n , y ∈ ∆m such that neither
player can unilaterally modify their strategy to improve
their objective by more than ϵ.
In this paper, we consider the problem of computing
an ϵ-Nash equilibrium of a zero-sum game in a standard,
simple setting where the players have restricted access
to the payoff matrix A through a matrix-vector oracle
that, when queried at x ∈ ∆n and y ∈ ∆m , outputs
(Ax, A⊤ y) (Definition I.2). We call these queries matrixvector queries; implementing a query is equivalent to
fixing a pair of strategies and computing the expected
payoff of each action when the other player’s strategy is
fixed.
This setting is extensively studied. Since a matrixvector oracle for A yields access to the gradients of
fA (x, y) := y ⊤ Ax with respect to x and y, a variety of
gradient-based optimization methods apply in this setting.
The well-known multiplicative weight update (MWU)
method computes an ϵ-Nash equilibrium with Õ(ϵ−2 )
queries [4, 23, 34].2 In 2004, Nemirovski [41] introduced
the mirror prox method, which (when applied with the
negative entropy function as the regularizer) solves the
problem in Õ(ϵ−1 ) matrix-vector queries. Later, Rakhlin
and Sridharan [46] showed optimistic mirror descent also
solves the problem with Õ(ϵ−1 ) queries. Moreover, as
Nesterov observed in 2003 (although the journal version

The central result of this paper is that indeed, improved query complexities are obtainable! We present
a deterministic, Õ(ϵ−8/9 )-matrix-vector query method
that computes an ϵ-Nash equilibrium. This gives the

Is Õ(ϵ−1 ) queries for computing an ϵ-Nash equilibrium
asymptotically optimal?

A. Our results

Given the well-studied nature of zero-sum games across
optimization theory and algorithmic game theory and the
lack of improvements in the past twenty years, query
complexity improvements would perhaps be surprising.
Indeed, related results indicate potential challenges toward
improving. First, Daskalakis et al. [20] essentially showed
that any no regret online learning algorithm for zerosum games must have regret that scales as Ω(1/T )
in the number of rounds (see Section I-B for further
discussion). Hence, if one approaches the problem of
computing an ϵ-Nash equilibrium of a zero-sum game
by designing an online algorithm for minimizing the
regret of a zero-sum game, it is not possible to achieve a
query complexity better than O(ϵ−1 ) with this approach.
Second, if one takes the aforementioned approach of
reducing the problem to minimizing the Õ(ϵ−1 )-smooth
(in the ℓ1 -norm) smaxϵ′ function to O(ϵ)-accuracy, then
it is known that Ω̃(ϵ−1 )-gradient queries are required to
minimize a Õ(ϵ−1 )-smooth function in the ℓ1 -norm to
O(ϵ)-accuracy over the simplex in general [26].4 Finally,
it is known that Ω(ϵ−1 ) queries are necessary in the
worst case to approximately solve Lipschitz-continuous
variational inequalities, a problem which generalizes (1)
[1, 33, 44, 53]. All of these potential obstacles suggest
improvements may be challenging.
Naturally, given the fundamental nature of the problem
and the lack of improved methods or tight lower bounds,
information-theoretic lower bounds for zero-sum games
were recently studied in [32]. However, Kornowski and
Shamir [32] proves a lower bound of only Ω̃(ϵ−2/5 )matrix-vector queries against deterministic algorithms.

Lower bounds in the matrix-vector oracle model. As
mentioned, for ℓ1 -ℓ1 games (zero-sum games) Kornowski
and Shamir [32] recently showed a lower bound of
Ω̃(ϵ−2/5 ) queries. In addition, for ℓ2 -ℓ1 games, they
showed a lower bound of Ω̃(ϵ−2/3 ) queries. Their lower
bounds hold for all deterministic algorithms. For ℓ1 -ℓ1 games in particular, their work improved upon that of
[27], which showed a Ω(log(1/(nϵ))) lower bound for
sufficiently small ϵ = poly(1/n) and m = n. For ℓ2 -ℓ2
composite games, Liu et al. [35] showed a lower bound
of Ω̃(ϵ−2/3 ) against both deterministic and randomized
algorithms when the payoff matrix A satisfies ∥A∥F ≤ 1,
and Braverman et al. [6] showed a lower bound of Ω̃(ϵ−1 )
against both deterministic and randomized algorithms
when the payoff matrix A satisfies ∥A∥2 ≤ 1.
Other oracle models. Aside from the matrix-vector
oracle model, other more restrictive models have also
been studied in the optimization and algorithmic game
theory literature. Some prior works [11, 18, 25, 45]
consider a more restrictive setting where payoff matrix
access is restricted to row/column queries. Carmon et al.
[13] consider the case where payoff matrix access is
restricted to entry queries. Rakhlin and Sridharan [46]
and Daskalakis et al. [20] consider a “strongly-uncoupled”
online setting in which two players play a sequence
of strategies in rounds, {(x1 , y 1 ), (x2 , y 2 ), . . .}, and can
only query a matrix-vector oracle for the strategies that
were played in the history of the game; the goal is to
minimize the regret of the played strategies. Hence, the
strongly-uncoupled setting is more restrictive than the
setting which we study in this paper. In this stronglyuncoupled setting, Daskalakis et al. [20] showed a regret

C. Directions for future work
The obvious problem left open by our work is that of
closing the gap between our upper bounds (Theorems I.3
and I.4) and the lower bounds of Kornowski and Shamir
[32]. In this paper, we prove that improvements over the
Õ(ϵ−1 )-matrix-vector queries achieved by mirror prox
is possible. The next question is to study the optimal
information-theoretic complexity. We hope our work
enables further research on this problem.
We note that our work focuses on studying the
information-theoretic complexity of ℓ1 -ℓ1 and ℓ2 -ℓ1
games. We do not study the problem of obtaining algorithms with better runtime or improved parallelizability,
and we pose these as interesting problems for future
work.
Lastly, our improved bounds on the number of matrix
vector queries for solving matrix-vector games as well as
our further improvements based on different bounds on
the intput matrix A, indicate the potential to develop algorithms that leverage alternative structure to obtain better
ϵ-dependence for broader classes minimax optimization
problems. This may be another avenue for future work.
D. Overview of approach
In this section, we outline our algorithmic and analytical techniques. The starting point for our algorithms is
the classic mirror prox algorithm [41], which we describe
below.
The mirror prox algorithm. Let f, ϕ be any differentiable, convex-concave functions over X × Y where
X ⊂ Rn and Y ⊂ Rm are convex and compact.
Mirror prox is a natural extension of mirror descent
[42] for computing an ϵ-solution of the minimax problem
minx∈X maxy∈Y f (x, y) + ϕ(x, y) given gradient oracle
access to f (which maps (x, y) 7→ ∇f (x, y)) and explicit
access to ϕ.
To describe the algorithm, we briefly introduce some
notation. In the remainder of the paper, we use Z as
a shorthand for X × Y and let d := m + n. Further,
for any z ∈ Z, we use zx ∈ X and zy ∈ Y to denote
the first n and last m coordinates of z respectively. We
denote the gradient mapping of a differentiable function
h : Z → R by ∇± h. That is, ∇± h : Z → Rd is given
by ∇± h(z) := (∇x h(z), −∇y h(z)) where ∇x h and ∇y h
denote the gradient of h with respect to the first n and
last m coordinates, respectively.
Now, mirror prox can be described for general geometries Z via distance-generating function (dgf) setups,
defined as follows. The following definition is inspired
by [11].

In the special case of matrix-games, the objective
function of interest is f = fA , and a matrix-vector oracle
yields a gradient oracle for the objective function fA .
Indeed, when A is normalized appropriately (∥A∥max ≤ 1
for ℓ1 -ℓ1 games, ∥A∥2→∞ ≤ 1 for ℓ2 -ℓ1 games, and
∥A∥2 ≤ 1 for ℓ2 -ℓ2 composite games), it is known how
to configure the dgf setup (Z, r, ∥·∥) so that L = 1 and
Γ = Õ(1) (e.g., [11, 41]). Thus, mirror prox yields a
deterministic Õ(ϵ−1 )-matrix-vector query algorithm for
each of the matrix-vector games described in Section I-A.
In fact, as we will describe in more detail below,
mirror prox is known to attain the O(ΓL/ϵ)-matrix-vector
query complexity even if ∇± f is not L-Lipschitz so
long as the mirror prox triples (z t , wt , z t+1 ) in each
iteration t of (2) satisfy a weaker condition called
L-local relative Lipschitzness with respect to ∇± fA
and (Z, ∥·∥, r) [19, Corollary 1]. The first key idea
in our approach is to carefully analyze—and capitalize
on—conditions where the triple (z t , wt , z t+1 ) does not
satisfy L-relative Lipschitzness with respect to ∇± fA
and (Z, ∥·∥, r) but still reveals useful information about
the payoff matrix A.

Note that (5) ensures that the triple (z t , wt , z t+1 ) is
guaranteed to reveal a large component of the matrix
A! Although this is not directly valuable for making
progress in computing a solution to fA + ϕ, it is valuable
in learning the payoff matrix A!
To capitalize on the information revealed in these steps
where (4) does not hold, we modify such iterations to
implement what we call model-update steps: we use O(1)
matrix-vector queries to detect when (5) holds and when
it does, use an additional O(1) matrix-vector queries to
project off and store a large component of the matrix
A. (We do this by subtracting from the matrix A in the
objective and then adding to an extra composite term—
see Section 3 of the full version of the paper.)
This projection reduces the Frobenius norm of A by
an amount depending on L′ , and therefore we can bound
the total number of model-update steps. Said differently,
in the remainder of the algorithm, we no longer need to
query the matrix-vector oracle over the subspace spanned
by the stored directions, and thus, the total number
of model-update steps can be bounded. By carefully
selecting L′ = ϵ1/3 and setting the step size of our prox
steps to 1/λ = 1/L′ , we optimally trade-off the number
of progress steps with the number of model-update steps,
thereby obtaining a query complexity of Õ(ϵ−2/3 ).
To summarize: in progress iterations, our algorithm
makes large progress by treating the function fA as
smoother than it might actually be, but performs a modelupdate iteration every time it discovers a large component
certifying otherwise. Inspired by related work in nonconvex optimization [10], we term this principle “smoothuntil-proven-guilty” and call our method “smooth-untilproven-guilty mirror prox.” We note that alternatively, one
could instead try to find model-update directions using
techniques from randomized numerical linear algebra
(see e.g., [5, 40] and references therein); however, the

Said differently, one way of interpreting our result for
ℓ2 -ℓ2 composite games is the following: The smoothness
of ℓ2 -ℓ2 composite games depends on the operator norm
∥A∥2 . If we further know that the Frobenius norm is
bounded ∥A∥F ≤ 1, then even though ∥A∥2 could
be as large as 1 in the worst-case, we can still bound
the number of low-rank projections necessary in order
to reduce the operator norm. Once the operator norm
has been sufficiently reduced, the problem is smoother,
and mirror prox is guaranteed to converge in fewer
iterations. Concretely, our method for ℓ2 -ℓ2 composite
games performs O(∥A∥2F /L′2 )-model-update iterations
and at most O(L′ /ϵ)-progress iterations to achieve an

In this paper, we do not directly present this ballacceleration approach but instead present a primal-dual
